questions.stem:
In a rustc diagnostic, what does a ---- underline mark?

rust
3 |     let first = &names[0];
  |                  ----- immutable borrow occurs here
4 |     names.push(String::from("corro"));
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here

options.text: A less serious version of the same problem
A secondary span — another place that participates in the error
A suggested replacement for that line
A warning attached to the error

questions.why:
^^^^ is the primary span: where the compiler gave up. ---- marks secondary spans: the other facts that made giving up necessary. Here push carries the carets, but push is not wrong — it is wrong given the borrow on line 3.

C is the tempting one because rustc does sometimes print suggested lines with + and - markers under a help:. Those live in a separate block with their own gutter. Inside the quoted source, ---- is always a secondary span.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0596]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     v.push(4);
  |     ^ cannot borrow as mutable
  |
help: consider changing this to be mutable
  |
2 |     let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
  |         +++

What is actually wrong?

options.text: Vec does not have a push method
The binding was declared let v, and push needs &mut self
v was moved earlier in the function
push requires the vector to be behind a reference

questions.why:
push takes &mut self, so calling it requires a unique borrow of v — and you can only take &mut from a binding declared mut. The primary span is on v, not on push, because the binding is the thing lacking permission.

Note that mutability is a property of the binding, not the type. Nothing about Vec<i32> changes; let mut v simply grants the ability to hand out &mut to it. This is also the one error where the help: diff is essentially always right.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0507]: cannot move out of `u.name` which is behind a shared reference
 --> src/main.rs:2:31
  |
2 | fn take(u: &User) -> String { u.name }
  |                               ^^^^^^ move occurs because `u.name` has type
  |                                      `String`, which does not implement `Copy`
  |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable

Which reading is correct?

options.text: You only borrowed the User, so you may look at name but not take it out
String fields cannot be returned from functions
User is missing a #[derive(Clone)]
The reference u needs a lifetime annotation

questions.why:
A borrow is permission to look, not to dismantle. Moving name out would leave the caller's User with a hole in it — a partially destroyed value the caller still owns — so it is forbidden through any &T.

The help: offers .clone(), which compiles and is sometimes right. But three other answers exist and are often better: return &str instead of String, take self by value if the caller is finished with the User, or use std::mem::take if you own a &mut and are happy to leave Default behind.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0597]: `s` does not live long enough
  |
4 |         let s = String::from("hi");
  |             - binding `s` declared here
5 |         r = &s;
  |             ^^ borrowed value does not live long enough
6 |     }
  |     - `s` dropped here while still borrowed
7 |     println!("{r}");
  |                - borrow later used here

Which marker tells you why the borrow was still required?

options.text: binding s declared here
borrowed value does not live long enough
s dropped here while still borrowed
borrow later used here

questions.why:
The later used here label is the one that closes the argument. Without a use after the block, the borrow would already be dead when s dropped and there would be no error at all — borrows end at their last use, not at a closing brace.

C is the tempting answer because it names the moment of conflict. It is real evidence, but it only matters because of line 7. In every borrow diagnostic, find the later used here marker first and ask whether that use can move earlier or disappear.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0308]: `if` and `else` have incompatible types
  |
3 |     let x = if n > 2 { "big" } else { 0 };
  |                        -----          ^ expected `&str`, found integer
  |                        |
  |                        expected because of this

Why does the arrow point at 0 rather than at "big"?

options.text: Integers are never valid in an if expression
The first arm sets the expectation; the second is the first one to violate it
0 is the last thing on the line
&str outranks integers in type inference

questions.why:
An if is an expression, so both arms must have one type. rustc types the first arm, records &str as the expectation — that is the expected because of this secondary — and then reports the first arm that does not match.

Which means the arrow location is about order, not about blame. Swap the arms and the error moves to "big". This is the general shape of E0308: the secondary marker says where the expectation came from, and it is usually the half worth reconsidering.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0599]: no method named `describe` found for reference `&T` in the
              current scope
help: consider restricting type parameter `T`

Retry implements Describe, and describe is spelled correctly. What is wrong?

options.text: The trait needs to be pub
describe should take self rather than &self
The generic function's signature does not require T: Describe
The impl Describe for Retry block is in the wrong module

questions.why:
A generic function is type-checked once, knowing only what its signature declares about T. Here that is nothing, so T might be u8, and u8 has no describe. The impl Describe for Retry is never consulted, because the compiler is not looking at Retry yet.

consider restricting type parameter T is the tell. Whenever E0599 offers that help, the method exists and a trait bound is missing. Adding <T: Describe> is a promise about every future caller, which is why the compiler can then trust the call.

questions.stem: E0599 "no method named X found" can mean which of these? Choose all that apply.

options.text: A trait bound is missing on a generic parameter
The trait is implemented but not imported into scope
You misspelled the method name
The receiver is a different type than you think it is
The method exists but is private, so it needs pub

questions.why:
A, B and C are the three headline causes and the help: line distinguishes them. D is the quiet fourth: .iter() gives you &T, not T, and a method taking self will not be found on a reference.

B is the one that catches everyone once. write!(f, "hi") on a File fails with E0599 until use std::io::Write; is at the top — the trait was always implemented, you just had not imported the vocabulary to name it.

E describes E0624, a different code. Privacy errors say "private", not "not found".

questions.stem:
Two errors are reported. Which do you investigate first?

rust
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:18
  |
3 |     let n: i32 = path.to_str().unwrap();
  |                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `i32`, found `&str`

error[E0599]: no method named `push` found for type `i32`
 --> src/main.rs:5:26

options.text: The E0308, because the E0599 is probably a consequence of it
The E0599, because it is nearer the code you last edited
Either — they are independent
The last one, since the compiler reports the deepest problem last

questions.why:
n is only an i32 because of the annotation on line 3. Fix that annotation and the type of n changes, so the second error changes or vanishes entirely. Chasing it first means debugging a phantom.

D is a real habit worth unlearning, and it comes from terminals: you see the end of the output, so the last error and the summary line are what is on screen. Scroll up, or pipe through head. Five errors regularly collapse to one.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
  |
1 | fn longer(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |                                ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
  = help: this function's return type contains a borrowed value, but the
          signature does not say whether it is borrowed from `a` or `b`

What is the compiler actually asking for?

options.text: Syntax — it just needs a 'a written somewhere
A decision about which input the returned reference borrows from
Proof that both arguments outlive the function call
String instead of &str, since references cannot be returned

questions.why:
'a is a claim, not decoration: it records that the result stays valid only as long as the input tagged 'a. Callers rely on it and the compiler checks it from both sides.

Lifetime elision would have written this for you given one input reference, or a &self. Two candidates and no self is exactly the case the rules refuse to guess, because guessing wrong hands a caller a dangling reference.

D is wrong here but right in the neighbouring case: if the reference pointed at something created inside the function, no annotation could save it and E0515 would be the error.

questions.stem:
rust
warning: unused `Result` that must be used
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
3 |     File::create("x");
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: this `Result` may be an `Err` variant, which should be handled

Why is this worth more than a warning's usual attention?

options.text: It always means the program will panic later
An ignored Result is a silently swallowed failure
It indicates a memory leak
It means File::create was called with the wrong arguments

questions.why:
Nothing crashes. The file simply is not created, the program continues as if it were, and the failure surfaces somewhere unrelated much later. unused_must_use is a genuine bug class, not style, which is why Result carries #[must_use].

The same trap hides in writeln! and flush, both of which return Result — dropping those is how data fails to reach disk.

Note that the help: here suggests let _ = File::create("x");. That silences the warning by asserting you meant to ignore it, which is a legitimate answer only when you genuinely did.

questions.stem: What is the difference between note: and help: in a diagnostic?

options.text: note: is more severe than help:
note: states a fact; help: proposes a change that may or may not be right
help: only appears when rustc is confident of the fix
They are interchangeable labels for the same thing

questions.why:
note: is always true and asks nothing of you — move occurs because s has type String, which does not implement Copy, or required by a bound in collect. The real explanation lives there.

help: is a suggestion optimised for making the error disappear, not for making your program right. When it proposes .clone(), it is proposing an allocation to end an ownership argument you have not had yet. Reading help: before note: is how codebases end up with .clone() on every line.

questions.stem:
rust
error[E0603]: unit struct `Conn` is private
 --> src/main.rs:2:27
  |
2 | fn main() { let _c = net::Conn; }
  |                           ^^^^ private unit struct
  |
note: the unit struct `Conn` is defined here

What does this tell you that E0433 would not?

options.text: The item exists and the path is correct — only visibility is blocking you
The module net does not exist
Conn needs to be constructed with Conn {}
You are missing a use statement

questions.why:
E0603 is good news disguised as an error: the name resolved. The compiler found exactly the item you meant, and the note: even points at its definition. One pub fixes it.

E0433 is the different failure — the path did not resolve at all, which means a wrong module, a missing crate, or a typo. Distinguishing the two saves real time: E0603 says "add pub", E0433 says "you are looking in the wrong place".

questions.stem: E0277 fires from deep inside a standard library call. Which line of the diagnostic is most likely to explain it?

options.text: The headline the trait bound ... is not satisfied
The --> file and line
note: required by a bound in ...
The For more information footer

questions.why:
required by a bound in ... names who wanted the trait — usually a library function several layers below your code. Without it you know a bound failed but not which call imposed it; with it, the requirement has an address you can go and read.

The headline is true and abstract. In practice E0277 usually means one of: an owned value passed where a reference was wanted (or the reverse), {} used on a type that only has Debug, ? on an Option in a function returning Result, or collect asked for a container it cannot build from that iterator.

questions.stem: You hit an error code you have never seen. What is the highest-value first move?

options.text: Search the web for the error code
Apply the help: suggestion and see whether it compiles
Read the headline as a claim, then find the primary span and ask what would have to be true for the claim to hold
Run rustc --explain on the code

questions.why:
C is the method and D is the reference. rustc --explain E0507 prints a minimal broken example, a fixed one, and the rule — offline, instant, and better written than most of what a search returns.

B is the habit this unit exists to break. It works often enough to feel like a technique and teaches you nothing, and when the suggestion is .clone() it converts a design question into a permanent allocation.

A is fine later. It tends to surface someone else's differently-shaped problem with the same code, which is a slower path than the two the compiler ships with.

questions.stem: Why is #![deny(warnings)] a bad idea in a published crate?

options.text: It makes compilation significantly slower
New rustc releases add lints, so code that built in April fails in July — for everyone depending on you
It disables Clippy
It is ignored by cargo anyway

questions.why:
Lints are added and tightened with every release. A crate-wide deny(warnings) means a compiler you never tested against can break your users' builds, with nothing about their program having changed and no fix available to them.

Put -D warnings in CI instead: identical enforcement on your own machines, failing your build rather than theirs. The same instinct applies to #[allow(...)] — prefer the narrowest scope that works, on the item rather than the crate, with a comment saying why. A crate-wide allow hides the next real one.
